new_statements.quote: Kum 2002: 21: "This is necessary because Naki is a tone language. This implies the language uses tones to distinguish the meaning of words. Our goal in this chapter, therefore is to determine pertinent tones on Naki. [...] There are basically two types of tones in Naki, These are level and contour tones. [...] In Naki two level tones have been attested. They are a high tone and a low tone." | Good et al. 2011: 154: "There is clear evidence for the presence of four tone levels in Naki, as exemplified by the set of words gí 'egg', lī 'tongue', shè 'fowl', and mȕ 'person'. [...] Contour tones are also frequently encountered"

new_statements.rule_in_words: Naki (the described language closest to, and per Good 2010 probably the same language as, Mashi [jms]) is analysed purely as a lexical/grammatical tone language (Kum: H, L, LH, HL tonemes on every vowel and syllabic nasal; Good et al.: four levels plus contours); neither description mentions word stress or accent at all, so no stress position is stated anywhere.
new_statements.exceptions: None; no stress discussion exists. (Good et al. note class prefixes carry only lower tones, partly predictable from the stem tone; Kum notes tone marks number on nouns and tense on verbs.)
new_statements.domain_note: Both descriptions concern the Mekaf variety of Naki in Cameroon (naki1238), elicited citation forms and short texts; nothing is said about the Nigerian Mashi [jms] locality, for which only Koops's 1971 wordlist exists.
new_statements.identity_note: No linguistic description of Mashi (Nigeria) [jms] itself exists beyond Koops's 1971 'Mairago-Mashi' wordlist (Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description = wordlist; scan held privately by Glottolog). Glottolog 5.x groups jms with Naki [mff] (naki1238) as 'Nakic'; Good (2010: fn. 2) writes that jms 'is probably a variety of Naki'; Ethnologue 14 (2005 capture) places it in 'Taraba State, near Takum', Beboid, no population estimate. Everything quoted about phonology is from descriptions of NAKI, Mekaf variety (Cameroon, glottocode naki1238): Kum 2002 and Good et al. 2011. Note there is also a Naki-speaking village called Mashi inside Lower Fungom (Cameroon), which is NOT the Nigerian jms locality (6.92N 10.28E, Takum/Baissa area); the 'Mashi (Naki)' wordlist in Brye & Brye's Eastern Beboid lexicostatistics and the 'Marshi' consultant in Kum 2002 most likely refer to the Cameroonian village. A naki1238 check folder already exists, so cataloguing these Naki sources under mash1269 would double-count one described entity.

sources.locator: Kum 2002: p. 21 (PDF p. 31; page image pages/); Good et al. 2011: p. 154, section 3.7.2.3 'Tones' ('=== PAGE 0154')
sources.note: Nothing. Ch. 1 (p. 21ff) 'Naki is a tone language': two level tones (H, L) and two contours (LH, HL) established as tonemes; ch. 4 syllables ('the centre or nucleus of the syllable is indicated by a tone', p. 61); ch. 5 tone distribution and grammatical function (number, tense). No section or remark on stress/accent anywhere in the TOC or text. Describes the Mekaf variety (consultants from Mekaf, one from 'Marshi', one from Nser).

sources.note: Introduction (p. 1): 'The 225 wordlist from the two speakers of Mashi exhibits similarities and differences in vowels, consonants, affixation, whole word and tonal nuances.' Then tone-marked forms (nouns sg/pl, verbs in three TAM forms, numerals, pronouns) for two speakers and a closing 'Remark' comparison table. No tone inventory statement and nothing on stress/accent. The PDF text layer garbles the tone letters (custom font).
